title: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to an Annual nrl ref Salary
description: Learn how to convert an hourly wage to an annual nrl ref salary using the standard 38-hour week. Includes tax, Medicare, super, and award rate guidance from Fair Work.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top and tax deducted according to the 2026–27 resident scale.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the base rate for award/agreement-free employees, currently $26.44 per hour ($1004.90 per week for 38 hours). Award rates are higher minimums set by industry or occupation, found in pay guides from the Fair Work Ombudsman. Most employees are covered by an award, so their minimum pay is often above the National Minimum Wage.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my annual nrl ref salary?
faqs.a: Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. For example, the casual National Minimum Wage is $33.05 per hour. When calculating an annual nrl ref salary for a casual role, you multiply the casual rate (including loading) by 38 hours and 52 weeks. The loading compensates for not receiving paid leave entitlements.

faqs.q: Does the annual nrl ref salary include superannuation?
faqs.a: No. Superannuation is paid on top of your gross salary. The super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings (up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year). So if your annual nrl ref salary is $60,000, your employer must also contribute $7,200 to your super fund, making total employment cost $67,200.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the hourly to annual conversion

When you see an **nrl ref salary** figure, it typically represents the annualised equivalent of your hourly rate assuming a standard full-time week. The basic formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For most full-time roles, the standard week is 38 hours. This is the figure used by the Fair Work Commission for the National Minimum Wage and by many awards. If you work a different number of hours each week, the annual estimate will vary. The calculator on [the timesheet](/) uses this assumption unless you adjust the hours.

### National Minimum Wage example

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1004.90 per week for 38 ordinary hours. The annual nrl ref salary for this rate is:

$26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44

If you are a casual employee, a 25% loading applies, making the rate $33.05 per hour. The annual nrl ref salary for a casual on the minimum wage is:

$33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80

This loading is added on top of the base rate; never type a rate that already includes casual loading into the calculator.

## The role of awards and agreements

Most employees are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates than the National Minimum Wage. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes [pay guides](/blog) for each award, which include minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. These guides are updated after annual wage reviews. For example, the Supported Employment Services Award pay guide includes changes from 30 June 2026 and 1 July 2026.

If you are paid an annualised wage or salary under an award, your employer must ensure it covers all entitlements such as penalties, overtime, and allowances. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that annualised wage arrangements must be reviewed every 12 months to confirm the employee received at least the award minimum.

## Tax and Medicare on your annual salary

Once you have your annual nrl ref salary, you can estimate your take-home pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, the Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. For singles earning below a certain threshold (based on the 2025–26 reduction thresholds), the levy may be reduced or waived. The calculator on [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) applies these rates to give you an estimate after tax and Medicare.

### Example: $80,000 annual nrl ref salary

- Tax: $5,092 + 30% of ($80,000 – $45,000) = $5,092 + $10,500 = $15,592
- Medicare levy: $80,000 × 2% = $1,600
- Total deductions: $17,192
- Estimated take-home: $62,808 per year, or $1,207.85 per week

## Superannuation is paid on top

Your employer must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. This is paid on top of your gross salary, not deducted from it. So if your annual nrl ref salary is $80,000, your employer contributes an additional $9,600 to your super fund. The [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page explains how salary packaging can affect this.

## Putting it together: the nrl ref salary

When comparing job offers, the nrl ref salary is a useful benchmark. It standardises hourly, weekly, and fortnightly pay into an annual figure. For example, a fortnightly pay of $2,000 equates to an annual nrl ref salary of $52,000 (assuming 26 fortnights per year). The formula works both ways: if you know the annual figure, divide by 52 to get weekly, then by 38 to get hourly.

Remember that this calculation assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For more detailed calculations, use the [reference tables](/data) or the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page to check current rates.
